planting.note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings out around the last frost, or make a second sowing in early summer for a fall crop of baby leeks.

directions: Named for the Bulgarian city where the type originated, Varna is a quick-cycling summer leek prized for reaching usable size well ahead of longer-season winter storage leeks. Because it matures so fast, gardeners can crowd seedlings three or four inches apart and pull the whole planting young as slender, sweet salad leeks, or space them wider and let a portion size up into full stalks for cooking. The blue-green foliage tops slim, mild-flavored white shanks that blanch readily with light hilling. It handles a light frost but is best harvested through summer and early fall rather than overwintered, since it lacks the cold hardiness bred into dedicated winter leek types.

planting.note: Start indoors in modules and transplant out once seedlings are pencil-thick; can also be sown into an outdoor seedbed and transplanted later for a late-summer through early-winter harvest window.

directions: Jolant is a European mid-season leek bred to bridge the gap between quick summer types and the toughest overwintering varieties, giving a long stretch of harvest from late summer well into early winter. Plants form thick, well-blanched white shanks with a moderate flavor and hold in the ground without bolting or splitting for weeks once mature, which spreads out the harvest window instead of forcing a single cutting date. Moderate winter hardiness lets a fall-sown planting carry through the first hard frosts in milder climates, though it is not as cold-tolerant as dedicated winter leek strains. Hill soil around the base as the shanks thicken to maximize the tender white portion.

planting.note: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; the semi-bush habit tolerates somewhat closer row spacing than sprawling vine-type butternut.

directions: Betternut 401 is a commercial hybrid butternut bred by Rupp Seeds for growers who want the uniform tan fruit and deep-orange flesh of classic butternut squash without the full sprawl of open-pollinated vining types. Its semi-bush growth habit keeps vines shorter and more manageable, allowing tighter spacing and easier harvest while still producing well-shaped, roughly two to three pound fruit with a small seed cavity. The variety carries tolerance to powdery mildew and better resistance to fruit cracking than many older butternut lines, both of which support cleaner, more uniform fresh-market packouts. Cure fruit in a warm location for one to two weeks after harvest to firm the skin and concentrate sugars before storing.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost, giving the long, vigorous vines ample room to run; a sturdy trellis can support the developing fruit off the ground if garden space is tight.

directions: Canesi is an Italian heirloom in the butternut group, grown historically for producing unusually large, pale tan fruit that can dwarf standard butternut in size while keeping the same sweet, dense, deep-orange flesh. Vines are exceptionally vigorous and productive, so plants benefit from generous spacing or a strong support structure to keep the heavy fruit from resting directly on wet soil. Harvest once the rind has turned mostly tan with only faint traces of green remaining, since fruit picked too early lacks the full sweetness the variety is known for. Like other moschata squash, cured Canesi fruit stores well through winter in a cool, dry location.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; provide plenty of room, since vines are unusually prolific and can set eight or more fruit each.

directions: Chirimen is an old Japanese squash of the Yokohama group, named for its deeply ribbed, warty rind reminiscent of crinkled chirimen crepe fabric. Fruit starts dark green and ripens to a mottled bronze-orange, enclosing thick, moist, deep-yellow flesh with a sweetness similar to kabocha or butternut. The vines are extremely productive, often setting eight to twelve flattened, globe-shaped fruit weighing five to eleven pounds apiece over a season. Popular in Japan since the Edo period, it is well suited to simmering in broth, roasting, or tempura once fully cured, and stores for months when kept cool and dry after harvest.

common_name: Running Conch Cowpea (Vining North Florida Cream Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has passed; give plants a trellis, fence, or tall companion crop to climb, since Running Conch retains the rangy vining habit of its 19th-century Florida ancestors rather than growing as a compact bush.

directions: Sow directly in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun, and let the long vines climb a trellis or scramble over corn or sorghum stalks in the old co-cropping style. Running Conch belongs to the Conch group of cream-seeded southern peas, first documented along the St. Johns River in north Florida in the late 1800s and likely introduced from the West Indies. The narrow, slender pods hold medium-sized cream-colored peas prized for a delicate flavor and notably fast, easy cooking compared with other dried peas. Harvest pods green for fresh shelling once they fill out, or leave them on the vine to dry fully for storage peas; like other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen and tolerates heat and drought well once established.
